predecessors.name: Seleucid Empire
predecessors.text: Parthia and Hyrcania, the satrapy of Andragoras, a Seleucid rebel who had 'proclaimed his independence' about 245 BC

successors.name: Sasanian Empire
successors.text: the Parthian outline of 224, passing to Ardashir's Sasanian Empire; the pages do not date the conquest of the rump

ledger.x: 238 BC: Arsaces I and his brother Tiridates I seize Parthia from Andragoras.
209 BC: Parthia submits to Antiochus III (bridged).
188 BC: Parthia is independent again.
163 BC at the earliest: Mithridates I invades Greco-Bactria.
158 BC: Mithridates I takes Aria and Margiana.
158 BC: the fighting with Eucratides ends with Aria and Margiana Parthian.
148 BC: Mithridates I takes Media.
148 BC: Atropatene is taken with Media ('conquering Media and Atropatene in 148/7 BC'); the atropatene dossier opens its contest the same year.
147 BC: Atropatene is subdued.
147 BC: Atropatene becomes a Parthian dependency under its own kings.
141 BC: Mithridates I takes Babylonia.
141 BC: the court turns west.
About 140 BC: Susa and Elymais become Parthian.
About 140 BC: Demetrius II tries to retake Babylonia, 'at first successful in his efforts to reconquer Babylonia'.
138 BC: Demetrius II 'was defeated and captured in 138 BC'; the Parthian Empire page says 140 BC for the invasion and its defeat.
The 130s BC: Persis comes under Parthia.
130 BC: Antiochus VII retakes Babylonia.
130 BC: Babylonia and Susa are lost to the Seleucid king Antiochus VII.
129 BC: Antiochus VII dies and Babylonia is recovered.
129 BC: the Seleucid campaign ends with Antiochus VII's death at Ecbatana.
About 127 BC: the east goes to the Saka.
By 122 BC: Characene's kings become Parthian vassals.
About 120 BC: Armenia accepts Parthian suzerainty.
By 115 BC: Mithridates II retakes Sakastan.
Before 115 BC (bridged): Mithridates II retakes Bactria and the middle Amu Darya from nomads.
113 BC: Dura-Europos.
About 95 BC: Mithridates II attacked Adiabene, Gordyene and Osrhoene and conquered them, moving the western border to the Euphrates; the kingdoms acknowledged his authority by 95 BC.
About 95 BC: Gordyene submits to Mithridates II (Adiabene, Gordyene and Osrhoene conquered).
About 95 BC: Osroene submits to Mithridates II (Adiabene, Gordyene and Osrhoene conquered).
About 96/95 BC: Tigranes, released by Mithridates II and made king of Armenia, 'ceded an area called seventy valleys in the Caspiane to Mithridates II'; Strabo says Tigranes took them back later.
About 87 BC: Tigranes ends his Parthian vassalage.
88-85 BC: Tigranes recovers the seventy valleys and 'retook Adiabene, Gordyene, and Media Atropatene'.
88-85 BC: Adiabene passes from Parthia to Tigranes.
88-85 BC: Gordyene passes from Parthia to Tigranes.
88-85 BC: Tigranes 'retook Adiabene, Gordyene, and Media Atropatene'; Atropatene passes under Armenian overlordship.
67 BC: Parthia attacks Gordyene.
66/65 BC: Phraates III takes Mesopotamia.
66/65 BC: Osroene leaves the Parthian sphere: it is the western district of Osroene, excluded from Phraates's Mesopotamia and a Roman dependency.
65 BC: the Gordyene dispute goes to Pompey: he 'offered arbitration between Tigranes and the Parthian king over Corduene'; Phraates's invasion of Armenia (c.

65 BC (bridged): after Pompey's settlement Tigranes keeps only 'the heartland of his kingdom' and 'all of his conquests were annexed', which does not name Atropatene; the page is silent on Atropatene after 66 BC.
63 BC (bridged): Cliopatria carves the Kingdom of Adiabene out of the Parthian land at -63.
54 BC: Crassus invades Mesopotamia.
53 BC: Carrhae.
40 BC: Pacorus and Labienus overrun Syria.
40 BC: the Parthians install Antigonus in Judea.
38 BC: Syria is recovered by Rome.
37 BC: Herod ousts Antigonus 'with Roman help', ending the Parthian client in Judea.
36 BC: Antony invades Media Atropatene.
36 BC: the invasion fails: Phraates IV ambushed his rear detachment and Antony lost much of his army in the retreat; no ground changes hands.
About 19 AD: Drangiana breaks away as the Indo-Parthian kingdom (bridged).
58 AD: the Armenian crisis.
63 AD: the Peace of Rhandeia.
115 AD: Trajan annexes northern Mesopotamia.
116 AD: Trajan takes Seleucia and Ctesiphon.
117 AD: Trajan dies and Rome leaves.
117 AD: northern Mesopotamia returns to Parthia.
161 AD: Vologases IV invades Armenia.
161 AD: Armenia under Vologases's king.
163 AD: Statius Priscus takes Artaxata.
165 AD: Rome keeps its gains in upper Mesopotamia.
165 AD: Cassius takes Ctesiphon.
195 AD: Severus invades Mesopotamia and occupies Seleucia and Babylon.
197 AD: Severus sacks Ctesiphon again and was 'unable to take Hatra'; the war gave Rome northern Mesopotamia 'as far as the areas around Nisibis and Singara'.
197 AD: Severus withdraws from Ctesiphon with northern Mesopotamia annexed.
215 AD: Persis passes to Ardashir.
215 AD: the frataraka kingdom of Persis, a Parthian client since the 130s BC, becomes Ardashir's own state.
224 AD: Ardashir's land by Hormozdgan.
224 AD: Characene leaves the Parthian sphere.
224 AD: Elymais (Susiana) leaves the Parthian sphere.
224 AD (bridged): the Parthian overlordship ends with the dynasty at Hormozdgan.
28 April 224: Ardashir I defeats and kills Artabanus IV at Hormozdgan, ending Parthian rule.

wars.name: Seleucid expedition of Seleucus II against Arsaces I
wars.outcome: The Seleucids recovered Parthia briefly: Arsaces made peace with the Greco-Bactrian ruler Diodotus II, withdrew to the Apasiacae, and later regained his territories.

wars.name: Mithridates I's war with Eucratides of Bactria
wars.outcome: Parthian victory: Aria, Margiana and western Bactria taken; Eucratides 'supposedly made a Parthian vassal'.

wars.name: Mithridates I's conquest of Media and Mesopotamia
wars.outcome: Media and Atropatene fell in 148/147, Babylonia in 141; Demetrius II was captured in 138.

wars.name: Antiochus VII's eastern campaign
wars.outcome: Antiochus VII retook Babylonia and Susa, then was killed at Ecbatana in 129 BC; the Seleucids lost the east for good.

wars.name: Mithridates II's Armenian and Mesopotamian campaigns
Tigranes the Great's reconquest
wars.outcome: Armenia 'retook Adiabene, Gordyene, and Media Atropatene' and the seventy valleys while Parthia was in its Dark Age after Mithridates II.

wars.name: Parthian attack on Gordyene and Pompey's arbitration
wars.outcome: Parthia took Mesopotamia except the western district of Osroene; Pompey arbitrated over Corduene; Phraates abandoned the siege of Artaxata.

wars.name: Crassus's Parthian campaign
wars.outcome: Parthian victory at Carrhae (53 BC): Crassus and his son killed, the eagles taken; no border change.

wars.name: Parthian invasion of Syria (51 BC)
wars.outcome: Pacorus and Osaces besieged Cassius in Antioch; Cassius ambushed them near Antigoneia and Osaces was killed; no border change.

wars.name: Parthian invasion of Syria and Judea
wars.outcome: Pacorus and Labienus held Syria and installed Antigonus in Judea; Ventidius won at the Cilician Gates (39) and Mount Gindarus (38, Pacorus killed); Herod ousted Antigonus in 37.

wars.name: Antony's Parthian War
wars.outcome: Antony's invasion of Media Atropatene failed after Phraates IV ambushed his rear detachment; no border change.

wars.name: Roman-Parthian war over Armenia
wars.outcome: Peace of Rhandeia (63): Tiridates and his descendants rule Armenia on condition that they receive the kingship from the Roman emperor.

wars.name: Trajan's Parthian campaign
wars.outcome: Trajan annexed Armenia (114) and northern Mesopotamia (115), took Seleucia and Ctesiphon (116) and reached Charax; revolts and the failed siege of Hatra forced a retreat; Hadrian gave up the conquests.

wars.name: Roman-Parthian War of 161-166
wars.outcome: Roman victory: Armenia 'reconstructed on Roman terms', Ctesiphon taken and burned in 165, 'Minor Roman gains in upper Mesopotamia'.

wars.name: Severus's Parthian war
wars.outcome: Severus occupied Seleucia and Babylon (195), sacked Ctesiphon (197) and failed at Hatra; Rome kept northern Mesopotamia as far as Nisibis and Singara.

wars.name: Caracalla's and Macrinus's Parthian war
wars.outcome: Caracalla sacked Arbela (216); Macrinus lost the battle of Nisibis (217) and paid Parthia over 200 million denarii; no border change.

wars.name: Ardashir's revolt and the Battle of Hormozdgan
wars.outcome: Ardashir took Persis (211/2), then Kerman, Isfahan, Susa and Characene, and defeated and killed Artabanus IV at Hormozdgan on 28 April 224; the Parthian dynasty ended.

certainty.note: No treaty or survey line in these centuries.
The Euphrates frontier with Rome after Hadrian is the page's 'limit of direct Roman control' but moved with every war (115, 117, 165, 197); the Kushan and steppe frontiers are approximate.
